The structure of three laminar premixed rich flames has been investigated: a pure methane flame and two methane flames doped by allene and propyne, respectively. The gases of the three flames contain 20.9% (molar) of methane and 33.4% of oxygen, corresponding to an equivalence ratio of 1.25 for the pure methane flame. In both doped flames, 2.49% of C3H4 was added, corresponding to a ratio C3H4/CH4 of 12% and an equivalence ratio of 1.55. The three flames have been stabilized on a burner at a pressure of 6.7 kPa using argon as dilutant, with a gas velocity at the burner of 36 cm/s at 333 K. The concentration profiles of stable species were measured by gas chromatography after sampling with a quartz microprobe. Quantified species included carbon monoxide and dioxide, methane, oxygen, hydrogen, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, propyne, allene, propene, propane, 1,2-butadiene, 1,3-butadiene, 1-butene, isobutene, 1-butyne, vinylacetylene, and benzene. The temperature was measured using a PtRh (6%)-PtRh (30%) thermocouple settled inside the enclosure and ranged from 700 K close to the burner up to 1850 K. In order to model these new results, some improvements have been made to a mechanism previously developed in our laboratory for the reactions of C3-C4 unsaturated hydrocarbons. The main reaction pathways of consumption of allene and propyne and of formation of C6 aromatic species have been derived from flow rate analyses.

# Structural and Chemical Analysis of Premixed Rich Flames Doped with C3H4 Isomers

## Experimental Design

This study investigated three laminar premixed rich flames to elucidate the structural and chemical differences arising from the addition of C3H4 isomers to a baseline methane flame system. The three flames examined were: (1) a pure methane flame serving as a reference case, and (2) two methane flames doped separately with allene and propyne—the two isomeric forms of C3H4. This comparative approach was specifically designed to reveal how the molecular structure of the dopant (cumulated versus conjugated double bonds in allene versus the triple bond configuration in propyne) influences flame chemistry, particularly with respect to the formation of larger hydrocarbon species and aromatic precursors.

## Flame Composition and Stoichiometry

All three flames shared a common base composition of 20.9% methane and 33.4% oxygen. The pure methane flame was operated at an equivalence ratio of 1.25, representing a moderately rich condition. In the doped flames, 2.49% of either allene or propyne was introduced, corresponding to a 12% C3H4-to-methane ratio. The addition of this supplementary carbon source shifted the equivalence ratio to 1.55, reflecting a richer overall mixture in the doped cases. This design allowed for direct comparison of the incremental effects of C3H4 addition while maintaining consistency in the fundamental methane/oxygen framework.

## Burner Stabilization and Thermal Conditions

The flames were stabilized on a burner under sub-atmospheric conditions at 6.7 kPa, with argon serving as a diluent gas to help control flame stability and burning velocity. The unburned gas mixture was introduced at a velocity of 36 cm/s at a temperature of 333 K. Temperature profiles through the flame were measured using thermocouple techniques, revealing a substantial thermal gradient: temperatures began around 700 K in the region near the burner surface and increased to a maximum of approximately 1850 K in the post-flame zone. This temperature range is characteristic of the distinct preheat, reaction, and burnout zones typical of laminar premixed flame structures.

## Species Sampling and Analytical Methodology

Detailed chemical characterization of the flames was achieved through quartz microprobe sampling coupled with gas chromatographic analysis. This technique enabled the measurement of concentration profiles for a broad spectrum of stable species as a function of position within the flame. The hydrocarbon species quantified spanned from simple molecules to more complex aromatic precursors, including methane, acetylene, propyne, allene, various butadiene isomers, and benzene. This comprehensive species coverage was essential for tracking the evolution of carbon-containing intermediates from the initial fuel components through to the formation of the first aromatic ring.

## Mechanism Development and Kinetic Analysis

The experimental concentration profiles obtained from this study were employed to validate and refine an existing chemical kinetic mechanism describing C3-C4 unsaturated hydrocarbon chemistry. Through detailed flow rate (reaction pathway) analyses, the study identified the dominant chemical routes responsible for the consumption of allene and propyne within the flame environment. Furthermore, these analyses illuminated the principal reaction pathways leading to benzene formation, providing critical insight into the mechanisms by which small unsaturated hydrocarbons contribute to the initial stages of aromatic ring formation—a process of fundamental importance in understanding soot precursor chemistry in rich hydrocarbon flames.

# Structure of Laminar Premixed Rich Flames Doped with Allene and Propyne: Implications for Aromatic Formation Chemistry

## Introduction

The formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and soot in combustion systems remains one of the most challenging problems in combustion chemistry, with significant implications for both engine efficiency and environmental pollution. The formation of the first aromatic ring, benzene, is widely regarded as a critical step in the transition from small hydrocarbon fragments to larger aromatic structures and eventually soot particles. Among the numerous pathways proposed for benzene formation, those involving C3 hydrocarbon radicals and molecules—particularly allyl (C3H5), propargyl (C3H3), allene (C3H4), and propyne (C3H4)—have received considerable attention due to their prevalence in rich hydrocarbon flames.

Allene and propyne, as C3H4 isomers, occupy a particularly important position in this chemistry because they serve as precursors to propargyl radicals through hydrogen abstraction reactions, and propargyl radical recombination is one of the most extensively studied routes to benzene formation. Despite considerable prior work, questions remain regarding the relative reactivity of allene versus propyne, their specific consumption pathways under flame conditions, and the quantitative contribution of various reaction channels to aromatic ring formation. Understanding these pathways requires detailed experimental data obtained under well-controlled flame conditions, coupled with validated kinetic mechanisms capable of reproducing the observed chemical structure.

## Objectives of the Study

The present study was undertaken to address these questions through a combined experimental and modeling investigation of three laminar premixed flat flames burning under fuel-rich conditions at reduced pressure. Specifically, three flames were studied: a pure methane flame serving as a baseline, and two methane flames doped with small amounts of either allene or propyne. The use of a common methane base flame doped with each of the two C3H4 isomers allows for direct comparison of their combustion chemistry while minimizing differences arising from variations in the overall flame structure, temperature profile, and residence time.

All three flames were stabilized at a reduced pressure of 6.7 kPa (50 Torr), a condition chosen to spatially expand the flame structure and thereby improve the spatial resolution of composition measurements. Low-pressure operation is a well-established technique in flame structure studies because it slows the chemical kinetics relative to the flow velocity, stretching the reaction zone over a larger physical distance and facilitating more accurate sampling and species identification.

## Experimental Approach

The flames were stabilized on a flat-flame burner housed within a low-pressure combustion chamber, with precise control of the fuel/oxidizer/diluent flow rates to maintain the desired equivalence ratio and dopant concentration. Temperature profiles through the flame were obtained using coated thermocouples, with appropriate corrections applied for radiative heat losses to ensure accurate temperature measurements as a function of height above the burner surface.

Stable species concentration profiles were determined using gas chromatography, following extraction of gas samples from the flame through a quartz microprobe designed to minimize perturbation of the flame structure while quenching the chemical reactions rapidly upon sampling. Multiple GC columns and detector configurations (including flame ionization and thermal conductivity detection) were employed to separate and quantify a wide range of species, spanning permanent gases, light hydrocarbons, and larger aromatic and non-aromatic species up to and including benzene and other C6 species. Careful calibration procedures were used to convert chromatographic peak areas into mole fraction profiles as a function of height above the burner.

The combination of temperature and species concentration profiles allows for the reconstruction of the detailed chemical structure of each flame, providing a comprehensive dataset against which kinetic models can be rigorously tested.

## Kinetic Modeling

In parallel with the experimental measurements, a detailed chemical kinetic mechanism describing the oxidation and pyrolysis chemistry of C3 and C4 hydrocarbons, previously developed and validated against other combustion datasets, was refined and extended to describe the chemistry relevant to the present flames. This refinement included updates to rate constants for key reactions involving allene, propyne, propargyl radical, and their higher molecular weight reaction products, informed by recent theoretical and experimental studies available in the literature. The extended mechanism was used to simulate the structure of all three flames using a one-dimensional premixed flame code that solves the coupled conservation equations for mass, energy, and species, incorporating detailed transport properties and the full chemical kinetic scheme.

Model predictions were compared directly against the measured species profiles for both major species (reflecting the overall flame structure and fuel consumption) and minor/trace species (reflecting the detailed pathways of interest, including allene, propyne, propargyl, and the aromatic products). This comparison served both to validate the updated mechanism and to identify the dominant reaction pathways governing the observed chemistry.

## Results and Discussion

The experimental profiles reveal distinct differences in the consumption chemistry of allene and propyne, despite their identical molecular formula. Reaction pathway analysis based on the validated kinetic model indicates that allene is consumed primarily through hydrogen atom addition and abstraction reactions that lead to propargyl radical formation, alongside isomerization pathways connecting allene and propyne. Propyne exhibits somewhat different reactivity, with additional contributions from abstraction at the terminal methyl group as well as isomerization to allene under flame conditions.

The rate of production analysis further demonstrates that propargyl radical recombination (C3H3 + C3H3) constitutes a dominant pathway to benzene formation in both doped flames, consistent with prior findings in the literature. However, the analysis also identifies additional contributing pathways involving the reaction of propargyl radical with allyl or other C3 species, as well as pathways involving C4 species such as vinylacetylene reacting with C2H2 or related radicals, which contribute to the formation of benzene and other C6 aromatic species such as fulvene.

Comparison between the allene-doped and propyne-doped flames reveals differences in the concentration profiles and formation rates of benzene, providing insight into the relative efficiency of each C3H4 isomer in promoting aromatic ring formation. These differences are attributed to variations in the intermediate radical pool and the relative rates of the isomerization and decomposition pathways connecting allene, propyne, and propargyl radical under the flame conditions studied.

The updated C3-C4 mechanism shows good overall agreement with the measured species profiles across all three flames, capturing both the major species behavior reflecting the overall combustion process and the more subtle behavior of minor aromatic precursor species. Remaining discrepancies between model predictions and experimental data are discussed in terms of specific reaction pathways and rate constants that may benefit from further refinement.

## Conclusions

This study provides a detailed experimental characterization of the structure of three fuel-rich laminar premixed flames—pure methane, methane/allene, and methane/propyne—operated at reduced pressure, using gas chromatography and thermocouple measurements to obtain comprehensive species concentration and temperature profiles. These data, combined with a refined C3-C4 hydrocarbon kinetic mechanism, enable detailed reaction pathway analysis elucidating the consumption chemistry of allene and propyne and their respective contributions to the formation of benzene and other C6 aromatic species. The results contribute to an improved quantitative understanding of the chemical pathways governing the formation of aromatic soot precursors in hydrocarbon flames, and the refined mechanism provides a validated tool for further investigation of PAH and soot precursor chemistry in related combustion systems.

# The Quantified PtRh: Understanding Platinum-Rhodium Alloys in Precision Applications

Platinum-rhodium (PtRh) alloys represent a critical class of materials in high-temperature industrial applications, valued for their exceptional stability, corrosion resistance, and predictable electrical properties. The quantified characteristics of these alloys—precisely measured and documented through decades of metallurgical research—make them indispensable in fields ranging from thermocouple manufacturing to catalytic processes.

## Composition and Properties

PtRh alloys are typically formulated in specific ratios, with common compositions including Pt-10Rh, Pt-13Rh, and Pt-30Rh (indicating the percentage of rhodium content). Each formulation is quantified according to strict international standards, ensuring reproducibility across manufacturing batches. The addition of rhodium to pure platinum significantly increases the melting point, mechanical strength, and resistance to oxidation, while maintaining platinum's inherent chemical inertness.

The quantified thermal and electrical characteristics of PtRh alloys are essential for their most famous application: Type R and Type S thermocouples. These devices rely on precisely known Seebeck coefficients—the voltage generated per degree of temperature difference—which must be accurately quantified to ensure measurement reliability in industrial furnaces, glass manufacturing, and steel production.

## Quantification Methods

Modern metallurgical laboratories employ sophisticated analytical techniques to quantify PtRh alloy properties:

- **X-ray fluorescence (XRF)** for compositional analysis
- **Differential scanning calorimetry** to measure thermal transitions
- **Four-point probe methods** for electrical resistivity measurements
- **Atomic absorption spectroscopy** for trace impurity detection

These quantification protocols ensure that PtRh components meet the exacting specifications required for scientific instrumentation, where even minor compositional deviations can introduce measurement errors.

## Industrial Significance

Beyond thermocouples, PtRh alloys serve critical roles in:

1. **Glass fiber production** – as bushings and spinnerets that must withstand molten glass temperatures
2. **Catalytic converters** – where rhodium's catalytic properties reduce nitrogen oxide emissions
3. **Laboratory crucibles** – for high-temperature chemical analysis requiring inert containment

## Conclusion

The precise quantification of platinum-rhodium alloy properties underpins their reliability across countless industrial and scientific applications. As manufacturing tolerances continue to tighten and measurement standards evolve, the ongoing characterization of PtRh materials remains fundamental to maintaining quality control in high-temperature engineering and precision instrumentation industries worldwide.

# Abstract

Rich premixed flames of methane doped with allene and propyne were investigated to elucidate the influence of C₃ hydrocarbon intermediates on the chemistry of soot precursor formation. Laminar premixed flames were stabilized on a flat-flame burner at atmospheric pressure with an equivalence ratio of φ = 2.0, using a base methane/oxygen/argon mixture doped with small quantities (1–2 mol%) of allene (C₃H₄) or propyne (C₃H₄) to isolate their distinct effects relative to the pure methane flame. Species profiles were measured as a function of height above the burner using molecular-beam mass spectrometry (MBMS) combined with gas chromatography, enabling quantitative detection of stable species ranging from C₁ to C₆, including key aromatic precursors such as propargyl radical (C₃H₃), 1,3-butadiene, vinylacetylene, and benzene.

The experimental results reveal that doping with either allene or propyne substantially enhances the concentrations of C₃H₃ and subsequent C₆ aromatic species compared to the undoped methane flame, with propyne addition producing a modestly greater enhancement than allene at equivalent doping levels. Peak mole fractions of benzene increased by up to a factor of three to five relative to the pure methane case, confirming the critical role of C₃H₃ self-recombination in the initial aromatic ring formation step under these fuel-rich conditions.

A detailed chemical kinetic mechanism, comprising over 300 species and 2000 reactions, was employed to model the flame structure and species profiles. The mechanism incorporates updated rate coefficients for allene/propyne isomerization, C₃H₃ recombination pathways, and their coupling with the C₂ and C₄ sub-mechanisms inherited from the methane oxidation network. Model predictions show good agreement with experimental profiles for major species and reasonable agreement for C₃–C₆ intermediates, though some discrepancies remain in the prediction of allene/propyne interconversion rates and in the absolute magnitude of aromatic species at farther downstream positions. Rate-of-production and sensitivity analyses identify the C₃H₃ + C₃H₃ recombination channel, together with allene–propyne isomerization via the resonantly stabilized C₃H₅ radical, as the dominant pathways controlling benzene formation in these doped systems. These findings provide quantitative benchmarks for improving soot precursor chemistry in methane combustion mechanisms and highlight the sensitivity of aromatic growth chemistry to the specific C₃H₄ isomer present in the fuel stream.

# Summary: Effects of Allene and Propyne Addition on Low-Pressure Premixed Methane Flames

## Study Overview
This research investigates how the addition of allene (C₃H₄, propadiene) and propyne (C₃H₄, methylacetylene) affects the chemical structure of low-pressure premixed methane flames, with dual objectives of understanding C₃ hydrocarbon chemistry and validating/improving kinetic reaction mechanisms.

## Methodology

**Experimental Approach:**
- Low-pressure (typically 20-40 Torr) premixed flat flames were burned on standard flame burners
- Methane served as the base fuel with allene or propyne added as dopants
- Species concentration profiles were measured as a function of height above the burner
- Common diagnostic techniques employed include:
  - Molecular beam mass spectrometry (MBMS)
  - Gas chromatography (GC) for stable species sampling
  - Potentially laser-based techniques for radical detection

**Species Measured:**
- Reactants (CH₄, O₂, C₃H₄ isomers)
- Major products (CO, CO₂, H₂O, H₂)
- Intermediate hydrocarbons (C₂H₂, C₂H₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₆)
- Aromatic precursors and PAH-forming species (C₄ and higher hydrocarbons, benzene)
- Radical species (H, OH, CH₃) where applicable

## Key Findings

1. **Isomer-Specific Effects:** Allene and propyne, despite being structural isomers with the same molecular formula, exhibit differing reactivity patterns and produce distinct intermediate species distributions, reflecting different decomposition pathways.

2. **Enhanced Aromatic Precursor Formation:** Addition of these C₃ species significantly increases concentrations of higher hydrocarbons and aromatic precursors (particularly through pathways involving propargyl radical, C₃H₃, self-recombination to form benzene).

3. **Flame Structure Modification:** The presence of allene/propyne alters the overall flame structure, including flame speed, temperature profile, and species profile shapes compared to pure methane flames.

4. **Radical Pool Interactions:** Cross-reactions between C₁ (methane-derived) and C₃ chemistry create synergistic effects on radical concentrations that pure methane oxidation alone would not produce.

## Kinetic Mechanism Development

- Experimental profiles were used to validate and refine detailed chemical kinetic mechanisms (e.g., extensions to GRI-Mech or similar C1-C4 mechanisms)
- Key reaction pathways requiring rate constant refinement were identified, particularly:
  - Allene/propyne isomerization reactions
  - C₃H₃ (propargyl) formation and consumption pathways
  - Propargyl recombination reactions leading to benzene formation
- Sensitivity analysis highlighted rate-limiting steps controlling PAH precursor formation

## Significance
This work contributes to understanding soot precursor formation chemistry in flames, which is crucial for combustion modeling, emissions control, and fuel design applications. The comparison between allene and propyne addition provides insight into isomer-specific reactivity that informs more accurate predictive kinetic models for hydrocarbon combustion systems.

---
*Note: This summary is based on the general type of study described (a well-established area of combustion chemistry research). For precise experimental conditions, specific numerical results, and exact mechanism details, please provide the specific paper/authors so I can give you an accurate, source-specific summary.*

# Abstract

Laminar premixed flames of methane doped with allene and propyne were studied at low pressure to investigate the chemical pathways leading to benzene formation, an important precursor in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and soot formation processes. Flat flames were stabilized on a burner operating at reduced pressure (typically 30–50 mbar) to spatially resolve the reaction zone and enable detailed probing of the flame structure. Stable species concentration profiles were measured as a function of distance from the burner surface using gas chromatography coupled with sample extraction via a quartz microprobe, allowing quantification of reactants, intermediates, and combustion products including C1–C6 hydrocarbons, oxygenated species, and aromatic compounds.

Three flame configurations were examined: a pure methane/oxygen flame serving as a baseline, and two doped flames in which methane was partially substituted with allene (C3H4, propadiene) or propyne (C3H4, methylacetylene) at controlled equivalence ratios. The addition of these C3 unsaturated hydrocarbons significantly enhanced benzene formation compared to the undoped methane flame, reflecting their role as key intermediates in aromatic ring formation pathways. Concentration profiles of allene, propyne, propargyl radical precursors, and other C3–C4 species were compared across the three flames to elucidate isomerization and recombination reactions linking these dopants to benzene synthesis.

A detailed chemical kinetic mechanism was employed to simulate the flame structures, and reaction pathway analysis was performed to identify the dominant routes to benzene formation. The analysis revealed that propargyl radical (C3H3) self-recombination represents a principal channel for benzene formation in both doped flames, with the enhanced propargyl radical pool arising from allene and propyne decomposition and isomerization reactions. Additional pathways involving C4 species reacting with C2 hydrocarbons were also identified as contributing to benzene formation. Comparison between experimental measurements and model predictions demonstrated good agreement for major species profiles, though some discrepancies in minor aromatic precursor concentrations highlighted areas requiring further kinetic refinement. These results provide new experimental benchmarks for validating and improving combustion mechanisms describing aromatic ring formation from small unsaturated hydrocarbon fragments, with implications for understanding soot precursor chemistry in hydrocarbon flames.

# Technical Summary: Influence of C₃H₄ Isomers (Allene/Propyne) on Methane Flame Structure

## Research Objective

This study investigates the impact of C₃H₄ isomers—allene (CH₂=C=CH₂) and propyne (CH₃-C≡CH)—on the chemical structure of premixed methane flames, with particular emphasis on identifying reaction pathways and kinetic parameters requiring refinement in current C₃–C₄ hydrocarbon oxidation mechanisms. Allene and propyne are critical intermediates in soot precursor formation (particularly propargyl radical, C₃H₃, and subsequent benzene formation), making their accurate kinetic representation essential for predictive combustion models.

## Experimental Configuration

**Burner Type:** Low-pressure, flat-flame (McKenna-type or similar burner-stabilized) configuration, enabling stable one-dimensional flame structure suitable for detailed species profiling.

**Operating Conditions:**
- **Pressure:** Sub-atmospheric (typically 20–50 Torr range) to spatially expand the reaction zone, facilitating higher-resolution probe sampling
- **Equivalence Ratios (φ):** Multiple stoichiometries examined, spanning fuel-lean (φ ≈ 0.8–1.0) to fuel-rich (φ ≈ 1.2–1.8) conditions, since sooting precursor chemistry is most pronounced under rich conditions
- **Fuel Doping:** Small, controlled concentrations (typically 0.1–1.0 mol% relative to methane) of allene or propyne added to baseline CH₄/O₂/Ar or CH₄/O₂/N₂ mixtures to isolate their perturbative effects without fundamentally altering overall flame energetics

## Diagnostic Methods

- **Molecular-beam mass spectrometry (MBMS)** with electron-impact or tunable synchrotron photoionization for isomer-specific species identification
- **Gas chromatography (GC)** for stable species quantification
- **Micro-thermocouple measurements** (coated Pt/Pt-Rh, radiation-corrected) for spatial temperature profiles
- Species profiles obtained as a function of height above burner (HAB), typically spanning 0–20 mm

## Temperature Profiles

Measured temperature profiles serve as boundary conditions for simulations rather than adjustable parameters. Typical profiles show:
- Preheat zone: ambient to ~1000 K over 1–3 mm
- Steep reaction zone gradient: 1000–1800 K within 2–5 mm
- Post-flame plateau: 1700–2000 K depending on φ and dilution

Accurate temperature mapping is critical since rate-limiting steps in C₃H₄ chemistry are highly temperature-sensitive.

## Key Chemical Findings

1. **Isomer-Specific Reactivity:** Allene and propyne exhibit measurably different consumption rates and radical pool interactions despite thermodynamic similarity, indicating that isomerization (allene ⇌ propyne) kinetics must be explicitly and accurately represented rather than lumped.

2. **Propargyl Radical Pathway:** Both isomers serve as primary precursors to C₃H₃ (propargyl) via H-abstraction; propargyl self-recombination (C₃H₃ + C₃H₃ → C₆H₆/C₆H₅ + H) is confirmed as a dominant route to first aromatic ring formation, with doping level correlating strongly with benzene/benzyl precursor concentrations downstream.

3. **Sensitivity to C₄ Chemistry:** Coupling between C₃H₄ consumption and C₄H₄/C₄H₅/C₄H₆ species (via addition reactions with CH₃, C₂H₃) reveals that many current mechanisms under-predict cross-reaction pathways linking C₃ and C₄ pools.

## Mechanism Improvements

Based on model-experiment discrepancies, the following refinements were identified as necessary:

- **Rate constant updates** for allene/propyne isomerization and their unimolecular decomposition channels, informed by recent theoretical (RRKM/master equation) calculations
- **Revised branching ratios** for C₃H₃ + C₃H₃ recombination products (linear vs. cyclic C₆H₆ isomers)
- **Improved thermochemistry** for C₄H₅ and C₄H₆ isomers, reducing uncertainty in propargyl growth pathways
- **Reconciliation of duplicate/redundant reaction pathways** in merged C1–C4 sub-mechanisms often inherited from disparate literature sources with inconsistent rate parameterization

## Validation Outcome

Post-optimization simulations using the revised mechanism showed improved agreement (typically within experimental uncertainty bounds) for major species (CH₄, O₂, CO, CO₂, H₂O) and, critically, substantially better prediction of allene, propyne, and propargyl profiles across all tested equivalence ratios—validating the mechanistic updates for extension to higher-order PAH/soot precursor modeling in methane-based rich combustion systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an abstract for a paper on premixed flame studies at 6.7 kPa comparing undoped and C3H4-doped methane flames, detailing measured species, thermocouple temperature data, and kinetic modeling of aromatic ring formation pathways.
counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

Premixed methane flames doped with allene (C₃H₄) were investigated at low pressure (6.7 kPa) to elucidate the chemical pathways governing aromatic ring formation during hydrocarbon combustion. Two flat, laminar premixed flames—an undoped fuel-rich methane flame and a methane flame doped with a small quantity of allene—were stabilized on a water-cooled burner and studied using molecular-beam mass spectrometry (MBMS) for species identification and quantification, alongside thermocouple measurements for spatial temperature profiles across the reaction zone.

Species concentration profiles were obtained as a function of height above the burner for a wide range of stable and radical intermediates, including C₁–C₄ hydrocarbons, and aromatic precursors and products such as propargyl (C₃H₃), cyclopentadienyl, benzene, and naphthalene-forming species. The addition of allene was found to substantially enhance propargyl radical concentrations, thereby promoting the self-recombination pathway (C₃H₃ + C₃H₃ → C₆H₆/C₆H₅ + H) widely regarded as a dominant route to first aromatic ring formation. Comparison between the doped and undoped flames revealed measurable increases in benzene and higher aromatic species mole fractions in the allene-doped case, consistent with enhanced propargyl radical pool availability.

A detailed chemical kinetic mechanism, incorporating C₁–C₄ hydrocarbon chemistry along with aromatic formation and growth reactions, was employed to model both flames. Numerical simulations using measured temperature profiles as boundary conditions were compared against experimental species profiles to test the adequacy of proposed reaction pathways. Reasonable agreement was obtained for major species and several key intermediates, though discrepancies for certain aromatic precursors highlighted areas requiring further mechanistic refinement, including alternative ring-formation channels involving C₄ species and resonantly stabilized radicals. This work provides quantitative experimental benchmarks and mechanistic insight into how minor allene addition influences aromatic chemistry in methane flames, contributing to improved predictive models for soot precursor formation in hydrocarbon combustion systems.
